corrections.where: Section 3.3, the list of forecasting trajectories
corrections.printed: There are several types of forecasting trajectories of CES depending on the particular value of the complex smoothing parameter: a flat line, exponential growth, exponential decline, a harmonic trajectory converging to zero and a diverging harmonic trajectory.
corrections.recorded: For $0 < \alpha_0 < 2$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast $w'F^{h-1}v_t$ follows one of five trajectories set by the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]]: a flat line, exponential growth, exponential decline, harmonic oscillation converging to zero, or diverging harmonic oscillation; on the line $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 = 1$ it oscillates with constant amplitude.
corrections.reason: The five types cover the parameter plane only for $0 < \alpha_0 < 2$ (see the corrections of the growth, decline and divergence conditions), and on the line $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 = 1$ the eigenvalues are complex with modulus exactly 1: at the stable point $\alpha_0 = 0.8$, $\alpha_1 = 0.2$ the forecast oscillates with constant amplitude, which none of the five types describes.

corrections.printed: When $\alpha_1$ is close to 1 the influence of $\hat{e}_t$ on $\hat{y}_t$ becomes minimal and the second smoothing parameter $\alpha_0$ behaves similarly to the smoothing parameter in SES.
corrections.recorded: When $\alpha_1 = 1$, [[D1:CES]] is simple exponential smoothing with smoothing parameter $\alpha_0 - 1$; when $\alpha_1$ is close to 1, it behaves like it over short horizons only.
corrections.reason: At $\alpha_1 = 1$ the correspondence is exact. Near 1 it holds only over short horizons: with $\alpha_0 = 1.24$ the response of the forecast to a unit error stays within 0.025 of 0.24 for 10 steps at $\alpha_1 = 0.99$ or 1.01, but drifts by 0.14 to 0.30 over 100 steps.

paper.summary: Exponential smoothing forecasts a series by first choosing a model: with or without a trend, with or without seasonality. This paper proposes complex exponential smoothing (CES), which uses complex variables, pairing each value with its forecast error, so that one model moves smoothly between a level and a trend as its smoothing parameter changes. It shows that CES can be stationary or non-stationary depending on that parameter, and that it corresponds to an ARMA(2,2) model whose coefficients are tied together. A seasonal version handles seasonality without seasonal indices, so model selection reduces to a choice between two models. On the series of the M1, M3, tourism and M4 forecasting competitions, CES was more accurate than exponential smoothing, ARIMA and the Theta method on most error measures, though not on all, and adding it to a combination of forecasts improved the combination.

definitions.definition: Complex exponential smoothing: a forecasting method that combines each past observation $y_t$ and its forecast error $e_t$ into the complex variable $y_t + i e_t$ and forecasts with an exponentially weighted sum of these values, $$\hat{y}_t + i\hat{e}_t = (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1) \sum_{j=1}^{t-1} (1 + i - (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1))^{j-1} (y_{t-j} + i e_{t-j})$$, or recursively $$\hat{y}_t + i\hat{e}_t = (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1)(y_{t-1} + i e_{t-1}) + (1 - \alpha_0 + i - i\alpha_1)(\hat{y}_{t-1} + i\hat{e}_{t-1})$$, where $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$ is the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]] and $\hat{e}_t$ carries the information on past forecast errors.

The smoothing parameter of [[D1:CES]], the complex number $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$; its real part $\alpha_0$ and imaginary part $\alpha_1$ are the two real parameters estimated, and they set how much of the past observations and of the past forecast errors is carried into the forecast.

The state $c_t$ of the [[D1:CES]] state-space model, which carries information on both its own previous value $c_{t-1}$ and the previous level $l_{t-1}$; it does not correspond to the trend component of exponential smoothing.

[[D1:CES]] extended with a second pair of level and [[D3:nonlinear trend]] states taken at lag $m$, the seasonal period, with its own [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]] $\beta_0 + i\beta_1$: $y_t = l_{0,t-1} + l_{1,t-m} + \varepsilon_t$, $$l_{0,t} = l_{0,t-1} - (1 - \alpha_1) c_{0,t-1} + (\alpha_0 - \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$$, $$c_{0,t} = l_{0,t-1} + (1 - \alpha_0) c_{0,t-1} + (\alpha_0 + \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$$, $$l_{1,t} = l_{1,t-m} - (1 - \beta_1) c_{1,t-m} + (\beta_0 - \beta_1) \varepsilon_t$$, $$c_{1,t} = l_{1,t-m} + (1 - \beta_0) c_{1,t-m} + (\beta_0 + \beta_1) \varepsilon_t$$.

claims.statement: Depending on the value of its [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]], [[D1:CES]] is a stationary or a non-stationary model.

relations.note: Exponential smoothing in a state space framework (ETS) gives 30 models with no, additive or multiplicative error, trend and seasonal components, among which a model is selected by an information criterion.
Identifying the presence and type of trend in exponential smoothing often leads to misidentification and poorly performing long-term forecasts.
The diverse trend alternatives of exponential smoothing in a state space framework make the selection of a model difficult.
Selecting the most appropriate exponential smoothing model is a challenging task.
Even when the components of exponential smoothing are identified correctly, the estimated smoothing parameters and the weights they imply can give poor forecasts.

checks.notes: From F=[[1,-(1-a1)],[1,1-a0]] the characteristic polynomial is lam^2-(2-a0)lam+(2-a0-a1) (sympy), so both eigenvalues are inside the unit circle exactly on the triangle a1<1, a1<5-2a0, a1>1-a0 and at least one is on or outside it elsewhere (200,000 random points, no mismatch). Both cases therefore occur, e.g. (a0,a1)=(1.5,0.9) stationary and (1.5,1.1) non-stationary. The resultant of the AR and MA polynomials of the underlying ARMA(2,2) is (a0^2+a1^2)(a1-1)(a0+a1-2), so the unstable AR root is not cancelled except on the line a0+a1=2 (at a1=1 the cancelled factor is not the unit root). The result does not need C25, which is disputed below.

claims.statement: [[D1:CES]] has an underlying ARMA(2,2) model whose coefficients $$\begin{aligned} \phi_1 &= 2 - \alpha_0 \\ \phi_2 &= \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 - 2 \\ \theta_1 &= 2 - 2\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \\ \theta_2 &= 3\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 - 2 - \alpha_0^2 - \alpha_1^2 \end{aligned}$$ are functions of the same two parameters $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$, so that the autoregressive and moving-average coefficients are tied together; $\theta_2$ is nonlinear in them.

checks.notes: Computed y_t=[1+B w'(I-FB)^{-1}g]eps_t with sympy: det(I-FB)=1-(2-a0)B-(a0+a1-2)B^2 and the numerator is 1-(2-2a0+a1)B-(3a0+a1-2-a0^2-a1^2)B^2, so all four coefficients are as stated under the convention (1-phi1 B-phi2 B^2)y_t=(1-theta1 B-theta2 B^2)eps_t; on simulated series for (a0,a1)=(1.3,0.8),(0.7,1.2),(1.9,0.4) the identity held to 1e-16. The paper's own route (B1)-(B4) divides by 1-a1 and is garbled in the text; the transfer-function route used here needs no such division. Not confirmed as worded: only theta2 is a nonlinear function of a0 and a1; phi1, phi2 and theta1 are linear (affine) in them, so 'nonlinear' holds for the map as a whole, not for each coefficient. At a1=1 and on a0+a1=2 the AR and MA polynomials share a factor, so the minimal model there is of lower order.

Check of the corrected statement. The four coefficients are unchanged and were reproduced before (sympy transfer function 1+B w'(I-FB)^{-1}g and simulated series). The new wording holds in every part: all four are functions of a0 and a1 only, (phi1,phi2) fixes (a0,a1) and hence (theta1,theta2), so the AR and MA coefficients are tied together, and theta2 is the one coefficient that is nonlinear (quadratic) while the other three are affine. As before, at a1=1 and on a0+a1=2 the two polynomials share a factor, so the ARMA(2,2) form holds there but is not minimal.

claims.statement: [[D1:CES]] is stationary, with both eigenvalues of its transition matrix inside the unit circle, when $\alpha_1 < 5 - 2\alpha_0$, $\alpha_1 < 1$ and $\alpha_1 > 1 - \alpha_0$.

checks.notes: The eigenvalues of F are the roots of lam^2-phi1 lam-phi2 with phi1=2-a0, phi2=a0+a1-2; the standard conditions phi1+phi2<1, phi2-phi1<1, phi2>-1 reduce to a1<1, a1<5-2a0, a1>1-a0 (sympy: p(1)=1-a1, p(-1)=5-2a0-a1, product of roots 2-a0-a1). Numerically, over 200,000 random (a0,a1) in [-3,6]x[-4,4] the spectral radius of F was below 1 exactly when the three inequalities held, so the condition is also necessary. The paper's Appendix C reaches the same system by a longer case analysis.

checks.notes: The discriminant a0^2+4(a1-1) is positive when a1>1, so both eigenvalues are real, and the characteristic polynomial at 1 equals 1-a1<0, so exactly one eigenvalue is above 1 and the other below 1. Checked symbolically and on every random draw with a1>1 (about 75,000 points), for any a0.

claims.statement: When $\alpha_1 > 1$, [[D1:CES]] produces a non-stationary trajectory.

checks.notes: Given C18, the forecast w'F^{h-1}v_t contains a term in lam1^{h-1} with lam1>1, which is non-zero unless the state lies exactly on the other eigenvector, so the trajectory does not settle (example a0=1.5, a1=1.1: 10, 10.3, 11.15, ... 19.36 over 12 steps). One exception for the generated series rather than the trajectory: on the line a0+a1=2 the persistence vector satisfies Fg=0, the explosive mode is not excited by the errors and, from a zero initial state, y_t is a stationary MA(1); no point of that line with a1>1 is in the stability region.

claims.statement: When $\alpha_1 = 1$, [[D1:CES]] is equivalent to [[D19:ETS(A,N,N)]].

checks.notes: With a1=1 the state equations become y_t=l_{t-1}+eps_t, l_t=l_{t-1}+(a0-1)eps_t, which is ETS(A,N,N) with smoothing parameter a0-1; c_t no longer enters l_t or y_t. Sympy confirms it on the ARMA side: AR=(1-B)(1-(1-a0)B), MA=(1-(2-a0)B)(1-(1-a0)B), leaving (1-B)y_t=(1-(2-a0)B)eps_t, the ARIMA(0,1,1) of ETS(A,N,N). The equivalence is for y_t; the unused state c_t keeps the eigenvalue 1-a0 in the discount matrix, so CES at a1=1 is stable only for 1<a0<2.

checks.notes: D=F-gw'=[[1-a0+a1,-(1-a1)],[1-a0-a1,1-a0]] has characteristic polynomial lam^2-theta1 lam-theta2 with theta1, theta2 of C5 (sympy, difference 0), and discriminant 8a1+4a0-4a0a1-4-3a1^2 as in paper (14). claims.statement: For $0 < \alpha_0 < 2$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast $w'F^{h-1}v_t$ follows one of five trajectories set by the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]]: a flat line, exponential growth, exponential decline, harmonic oscillation converging to zero, or diverging harmonic oscillation; on the line $\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 = 1$ it oscillates with constant amplitude.

about.subject: the CES point forecast
about.relation: follows one of five trajectories set by

checks.notes: The five shapes all occur (verified by eigenvalues of F and by iterating w'F^{h-1}v_t), but the forecast is not always one of them and the parameter conditions of C27, C28 and C30 do not select them as stated. Counterexamples: (a0,a1)=(2.2,1.2), inside the stability region, has eigenvalues 1.087 and -1.287, so the forecast is a sign-alternating term of growing amplitude on top of growth, which is neither plain exponential growth nor one of the other four; (0.8,0.2), also stable, has complex eigenvalues of modulus exactly 1 (a0+a1=1), an oscillation that neither converges nor diverges. Correct version: the shape is set by the eigenvalues (2-a0 +- sqrt(a0^2+4a1-4))/2 and by the state v_t; the five-way list holds for 0<a0<2 away from the boundaries a0+a1=1 and a1=(4-a0^2)/4, with the direction (growth or fall) depending on v_t.
checks.resolution: The authors corrected the claim (paper.published_as.corrections) and the checker checked the corrected statement again, confirming it.

checks.notes: Check of the corrected statement. For 0<a0<2 the eigenvalues of F put every value of a1 in one of the listed cases: a1>1 real with the root above 1 dominant (growth), a1=1 flat, (4-a0^2)/4<a1<1 real in (-1,1) with the positive root dominant (decline), 1-a0<a1<(4-a0^2)/4 complex of modulus below 1, a1=1-a0 complex of modulus exactly 1 (constant amplitude), a1<1-a0 complex of modulus above 1; 49,823 random points with 0<a0<2 gave no exception, and the boundaries a1=1 and a0+a1=1 were checked at a0=0.3, 1.0, 1.7. Two parts do not hold as worded. On the boundary a1=(4-a0^2)/4 the eigenvalue (2-a0)/2 is repeated and the forecast is (A+Bh)((2-a0)/2)^h: it goes to zero without oscillating, but it is a linear term times an exponential, not an exponential decline, so this boundary belongs to none of the cases unless 'exponential decline' is read loosely. The trajectory is also not set by the parameter alone: with a1>1, a state on the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue gives no growth (a0=1.5, a1=2.5, state (-0.686,1): -0.686, 0.814, -0.965, 1.145, an alternating divergence), and a zero state gives a zero forecast; the statement needs 'for all states except those on one line' or 'for a generic state'.

claims.statement: When $\alpha_1 = 1$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a flat line.

checks.notes: With a1=1, F=[[1,0],[1,1-a0]] and w'F^k=(1,0) for every k (sympy, k=0..3, and by induction since the first row of F is (1,0)), so the forecast equals l_t at every horizon, for any a0.

claims.statement: When $\alpha_1 > 1$ and $\alpha_0 < 2$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast grows exponentially in magnitude, upward or downward according to the current state.

checks.notes: For a1>1 the eigenvalues are real with lam1>1>lam2 (C18), but lam1+lam2=2-a0, so for a0>2 the negative eigenvalue has the larger modulus and the forecast is dominated by a sign-alternating diverging term, not exponential growth. Example inside the stability region: (a0,a1)=(2.2,1.2) gives eigenvalues 1.087 and -1.287 and, from v_t=(10,3), forecasts 10, 10.6, 11.88, 12.46, 14.14, 14.62, ... 24.3, 22.99; 525 of the random stable points with a1>1 behave this way. Correct version: when a1>1 and a0<2 the forecast is dominated by lam1^h and grows exponentially in magnitude, upward or downward according to the state v_t.
checks.resolution: The authors corrected the claim (paper.published_as.corrections) and the checker checked the corrected statement again, confirming it.

checks.notes: Check of the corrected statement. For a1>1 the eigenvalues are real with lam1>1>lam2, and a0<2 gives lam1+lam2=2-a0>0, so lam1 is the larger in modulus (27,981 random points, no exception); the forecast is A lam1^(h-1)+B lam2^(h-1), which grows like lam1^h with the sign of A. Not covered by the wording: A=0 when the state lies on the eigenvector of lam2, (lam2-1+a0, 1), including the zero state, and then there is no growth (decay if |lam2|<1, alternating divergence if lam2<-1, e.g. a0=1.5, a1=2.5). The growth is also asymptotic, not from the first step: a0=1.5, a1=1.1 from state (10,-40) gives 10, 6, 9, 8.1, 9.45 before rising. The statement is correct with 'eventually' and 'unless the state lies on the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue'.

claims.statement: When $(4 - \alpha_0^2)/4 < \alpha_1 < 1$, $\alpha_0 > 0$ and $\alpha_1 < 5 - 2\alpha_0$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast declines exponentially.

checks.notes: The stated interval makes the eigenvalues real and gives p(1)=1-a1>0, but that alone does not put them inside the unit circle: the statement omits the conditions a0>0 and a1<5-2a0 that the paper's (C7) carries. Counterexamples: (a0,a1)=(-1,0.9) satisfies 0.75<a1<1 and has eigenvalues 1.113 and 1.887 (exponential divergence); (3.5,0.5) has eigenvalues 0.851 and -2.351. With those two conditions added (they hold at every point of the stability region with a1<1, where also a0<2, so the dominant eigenvalue is positive) the claim is correct: no violation among the random stable points.
checks.resolution: The authors corrected the claim (paper.published_as.corrections) and the checker checked the corrected statement again.

checks.notes: Check of the corrected statement. The corrected conditions still do not confine the eigenvalues to the unit circle: an upper bound a0<4 is missing. Counterexample: (a0,a1)=(5,-5.1) satisfies (4-25)/4=-5.25<a1<1, a0>0 and a1<5-2a0=-5, and has eigenvalues -1.113 and -1.887; the forecast from state (10,3) is 10, -8.3, 3.9, 5.73, -25.4, 64.1, -139. Of 8,675 random points meeting the stated conditions in a0 in (-4,8), a1 in (-12,4), 6,591 had an eigenvalue outside the unit circle, all with a0>4; none of the 2,084 with a0<4 did. Correct version: add a0<4 (the paper's (C7) has 0<a0<4), which makes both eigenvalues real and inside (-1,1). For 2<a0<4 the negative eigenvalue dominates and the decline alternates in sign (a0=2.2, a1=0.5: eigenvalues 0.743, -0.943; 10, 8.5, 5.3, 4.89, 2.73, 2.88), so a decline without alternation needs 0<a0<2. My first report named only a0>0 and a1<5-2a0 as the missing conditions; that list was incomplete.

claims.statement: When $1 - \alpha_0 < \alpha_1 < (4 - \alpha_0^2)/4$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a harmonic oscillation converging to zero.

about.subject: the CES point forecast
about.relation: is a harmonic oscillation converging to zero

checks.notes: The upper bound a1<(4-a0^2)/4 makes the discriminant a0^2+4a1-4 negative, so the eigenvalues are complex conjugates with squared modulus 2-a0-a1, which is below 1 because a1>1-a0. The forecast is therefore a damped sinusoid; all 7,493 random points in the region had complex eigenvalues of modulus below 1, e.g. (1,0.5) gives 0.5+-0.5i.

claims.statement: When $\alpha_0 \ge 0$ and $0 < \alpha_1 < 1 - \alpha_0$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a diverging harmonic oscillation.

checks.notes: For a0>=0 the claim holds: a1<1-a0<=(4-a0^2)/4 gives complex eigenvalues of squared modulus 2-a0-a1>1. For a0<0 the interval 0<a1<1-a0 extends above (4-a0^2)/4 and the eigenvalues there are real: (a0,a1)=(-1,0.9) gives 1.113 and 1.887, an exponential divergence without oscillation. Correct version: add a0>=0, or replace the upper bound by min(1-a0,(4-a0^2)/4); the lower bound 0<a1 is not needed. All points of the stability region have a0>0.27, so the claim is correct there (no violation among the random stable points).
checks.resolution: The authors corrected the claim (paper.published_as.corrections) and the checker checked the corrected statement again, confirming it.

checks.notes: Check of the corrected statement. With a0>=0 and 0<a1<1-a0 (so a0<1) the discriminant satisfies a0^2+4a1-4 < a0^2-4a0 <= 0, so the eigenvalues are complex, and their squared modulus 2-a0-a1 exceeds 1. Complex eigenvalues leave no real invariant line, so every non-zero state gives an oscillation of growing amplitude; 817 random points in the region gave no exception. The only state for which nothing diverges is the zero state.

warrants.text: The seasonal model takes the level and nonlinear trend states at lag m instead of carrying a set of seasonal components, so there are no seasonal indices to renormalise. Since non-seasonal CES captures both level and trend series without a choice of trend form, the only choice left is whether to include the lag-m states.

With the imaginary part of the smoothing parameter equal to one CES is the local level model ETS(A,N,N); with it above one the forecasts grow exponentially, as in multiplicative trend models; and the flexibility of its trajectories lets it follow trends that the level and trend classification of exponential smoothing captures only with separate models.

Seasonal CES consists of two CES parts, one at lag 1 and one at lag m, and each part follows one of the CES forecast trajectories, so the seasonal part can grow, decline or oscillate in its own way. The non-seasonal level can become negative while the lagged level stays positive, and the two levels evolve independently, so the seasonal part can change its amplitude and shape without any change in the level of the series.

Non-seasonal CES has an underlying ARMA(2,2) model that is stationary or not depending on its complex smoothing parameter; by analogy, the authors state the same of the SARIMA model underlying seasonal CES. No stationarity condition is derived for seasonal CES.

The count follows from the model equations: each complex smoothing parameter has two real parts, each pair of level and nonlinear trend states needs initial values (m of each for the lag-m pair), and the error variance is estimated.

On the seasonal subset of the M1, M3 and tourism data, CES with its seasonal or non-seasonal form chosen by AICc has lower RMSSE and MASE than every seasonal ETS model, which the authors take to show that the criterion chooses the seasonal form when it is needed. This is an argument from the accuracy results only: no experiment compares the selection by information criteria with other ways of choosing between seasonal and non-seasonal CES.

CES has lower RMSSE than ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method on the M1, M3, tourism and M4 data and lowers the errors of the combination it is included in, which the authors take as evidence that it is robust, while acknowledging that it does not suit every forecasting scenario. Robustness itself is not defined or tested: no experiment examines how the accuracy of CES varies across conditions or departures from its assumptions.

limitations.statement: CES produces very large errors on a few series: on M1 series 47 it fails to identify the trend and its MSIS is 523.034 against 25.590 for ETS(M,N,N), which inflates its mean MSIS, and on the non-seasonal subset it fails on two series.
The parameter restrictions under which seasonal CES is stable are not derived.
The effect of the length of a time series on the accuracy of CES is not analysed.
CES is formulated only with an additive error term; a version with a multiplicative error term is not developed.
The 10 M4 series on which ETS broke down were excluded from the M4 comparison, so the series were selected on the failure of one of the compared methods.
